meta.author: Abhijit Prakash Gawankar

questions.question: What is JavaScript?
questions.answer:
JavaScript is a high-level, dynamically typed programming language used extensively in browsers and also on servers through runtimes such as Node.js. It supports object-oriented, functional and asynchronous programming. In frontend development, JavaScript controls application behavior, UI state, API communication and browser interaction.
Example: React itself is JavaScript-based; React components, hooks and state logic ultimately execute as JavaScript.

questions.question: Difference between var, let and const?
What is scope?
questions.answer: Scope determines where a variable can be accessed. JavaScript has global scope, function scope and block scope. let and const respect block scope, while var is function-scoped.

questions.question: What is lexical scope?
questions.answer: Lexical scope means a function's access to variables is determined by where the function is written in the source code. A nested function can access variables from its outer lexical scopes.

questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.answer: Hoisting describes how JavaScript processes declarations before executing code. Function declarations can be called before their declaration. var is initialized to undefined, while let and const are hoisted but inaccessible before initialization because of the temporal dead zone.
questions.code:
sayHi();
function sayHi() { console.log("Hi"); }

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
questions.answer: The temporal dead zone is the period between entering a scope and the point where a let or const declaration is initialized. Accessing the variable during that period throws a ReferenceError.
questions.code:
console.log(x); // ReferenceError
let x = 10;

questions.question: What is a closure?
questions.answer: A closure is created when a function retains access to variables from its lexical scope even after the outer function has finished executing. Closures are useful for private state, factories, callbacks and function-based encapsulation.

questions.question: What is an execution context?
questions.answer: An execution context is the environment in which JavaScript code executes. It contains information such as variable bindings, scope information and the value of this. The global context is created first, and function contexts are created when functions execute.

questions.question: What is the call stack?
questions.answer: The call stack tracks currently executing functions. When a function is called, a stack frame is added; when it returns, the frame is removed. Deep or infinite synchronous recursion can cause a stack overflow.

questions.question: What is the difference between primitive and reference values?
questions.answer: Primitive values such as string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null and undefined are values themselves. Objects, arrays and functions are reference types in practical terms: variables hold references to objects. Assigning an object variable does not create a new object.

questions.question: Shallow copy vs deep copy?
questions.answer: A shallow copy duplicates the top level but nested objects remain shared. A deep copy creates independent nested structures. Spread syntax and Object.assign are shallow. structuredClone is a modern option for supported data.

questions.question: What is destructuring?
questions.answer: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into variables.
questions.code:
const user = { name: "Abhijit", age: 37 };
const { name, age } = user;

questions.question: Spread vs rest operator?
questions.answer: The syntax is the same, but the meaning depends on context. Spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements/properties. Rest collects remaining values into an array or object.

questions.question: What is this?
questions.answer: this is determined mainly by how a function is invoked. In a method call it normally refers to the object before the dot. call, apply and bind can explicitly control it. Constructors use it for the new instance. Arrow functions do not create their own this and capture it lexically.

questions.question: call, apply and bind?
questions.answer: All three can control this. call invokes immediately with arguments individually; apply invokes immediately with arguments as an array; bind returns a new function with this and optionally initial arguments fixed.

questions.question: What is a prototype?
questions.answer: A prototype is an object from which another object can inherit properties and methods. JavaScript uses prototype-based inheritance. When a property is not found on the object, JavaScript searches its prototype chain.

questions.question: What is the prototype chain?
questions.answer: The prototype chain is the sequence of objects JavaScript searches when resolving a property or method. It continues until the property is found or the chain reaches null.

questions.question: Are JavaScript classes real classes?
questions.answer: JavaScript classes provide class syntax, but inheritance is still implemented through prototypes. Classes make object-oriented code easier to express while the underlying model remains prototype-based.

questions.question: map vs filter vs reduce?
questions.answer: map transforms every item and returns an array of the same length. filter returns items that satisfy a condition. reduce combines items into one accumulated result.

questions.question: What is immutability and why is it important in React?
questions.answer: Immutability means creating a new value instead of directly changing the existing state object. React and Redux rely heavily on reference comparisons to detect changes efficiently. Immutable updates make state transitions predictable and easier to debug.
questions.code: setUser(prev => ({ ...prev, name: "Abhijit" }));

questions.question: Arrow functions vs regular functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions don't have their own this, arguments, super, or new.target — they lexically inherit this from the enclosing scope, so they can't be used as constructors and are a poor fit for object methods that rely on this. Regular functions get their own this (determined by how they're called), receive an arguments object, and can be used with new. Arrow functions also can't be generators.

questions.question: What is a higher-order function?
questions.answer: A function that takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both. They enable composition and abstraction over behavior — map, filter, reduce, and event-handler factories are all higher-order functions.

questions.question: What is currying?
questions.answer: Currying transforms a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument, returning a new function until all arguments are supplied. It enables partial application and reusable, specialized functions.

questions.question: What is an IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)?
questions.answer: A function expression that runs as soon as it's defined, creating an isolated scope. Before ES modules and block-scoped let/const, IIFEs were the standard way to avoid polluting the global scope and to encapsulate private state (the module pattern).

questions.question: Default parameters vs rest parameters vs the arguments object?
questions.answer: Default parameters supply a fallback value when an argument is undefined. Rest parameters (...args) collect any remaining arguments into a real array. The legacy arguments object is an array-like (not a real array — no map/filter) available only in regular functions, not arrow functions, and reflects exactly what was passed in, not the defaults applied.

questions.question: What is a pure function?
questions.answer: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and produces no observable side effects — no mutating arguments, no I/O, no reliance on external mutable state. Pure functions are easier to test, memoize, and reason about, which is central to React's rendering model and Redux reducers.

questions.question: What is a generator function?
questions.answer: A generator function (function*) can pause and resume execution using yield, returning an iterator. Each call to .next() runs until the next yield, making generators useful for lazy sequences, custom iterables, and — historically — flow control before async/await.

questions.question: Is JavaScript single-threaded?
questions.answer: JavaScript execution on the main thread is single-threaded, meaning one piece of JavaScript executes at a time on that thread. The runtime still provides asynchronous capabilities through browser or Node.js APIs, networking, timers and other mechanisms. Web Workers or worker threads can provide additional execution contexts for suitable workloads.

questions.question: Explain the event loop.
questions.answer: Synchronous code runs on the call stack. Asynchronous operations are handled by the runtime. When they complete, their callbacks are queued. Promise reactions are placed in the microtask queue. After the current task finishes, microtasks are drained before the runtime moves to the next task. The event loop coordinates this process.

questions.question: Microtask vs macrotask?
questions.answer: Promise callbacks and queueMicrotask are microtasks. setTimeout and similar scheduled callbacks are tasks/macrotasks. Microtasks are processed after the current synchronous task and before the next task, which affects execution order.

questions.question: What is a Promise?
questions.answer: A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It can be pending, fulfilled or rejected. It allows asynchronous work to be composed using then/catch/finally or async/await.
questions.code:
fetch("/api/users")
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(users => console.log(users))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

questions.question: async/await?
questions.answer: async/await is syntax built on Promises that makes asynchronous code easier to read. An async function returns a Promise. await pauses that async function until the awaited Promise settles; it does not block the JavaScript thread.

questions.question: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?
questions.answer: Promise.all succeeds only if every Promise succeeds and rejects when one rejects. allSettled waits for every Promise and reports each outcome. race settles when the first Promise settles. any fulfills when the first Promise fulfills and rejects only when all reject.

questions.question: Sequential vs parallel async operations?
questions.answer: If requests depend on each other, await them sequentially. If they are independent, run them concurrently with Promise.all to reduce total waiting time.

questions.question: What is debounce?
questions.answer: Debouncing delays execution until calls stop for a specified period. It is useful for search inputs where we do not want an API request for every keystroke.

questions.question: What is throttle?
questions.answer: Throttling limits how frequently a function can execute. It is useful for high-frequency events such as scroll, resize or mouse movement.

questions.question: Explain Redux.
questions.answer: Redux is a predictable state container. Components dispatch actions, reducers calculate new state, selectors read state, and middleware can handle cross-cutting or asynchronous workflows. The goal is predictable shared state, not putting every variable into one global store.

questions.question: What belongs in Redux?
questions.answer: Shared state that multiple distant parts of the application need can belong in Redux. Authentication state, shared lookups and cross-module business state are examples. Local form fields, modal flags or temporary component state often belong locally.

questions.question: Why should reducers be pure?
questions.answer: Pure reducers make state transitions deterministic and testable. API calls, timers and other side effects should happen outside reducers.

questions.question: What is Redux Toolkit?
questions.answer: Redux Toolkit is the recommended modern way to write Redux. It reduces boilerplate and provides utilities such as createSlice and createAsyncThunk while using Immer internally for convenient immutable update syntax.

questions.question: What are selectors?
questions.answer: Selectors are functions that read or derive data from state. They create a clear boundary between components and the store and can avoid repeated data-transformation logic.

questions.question: Redux vs Context API?
questions.answer: Context is useful for passing values through a component tree, especially relatively stable concerns such as theme or localization. Redux is more suitable when the application has complex shared state, many updates, derived data, middleware and a need for structured state transitions. They solve overlapping but different problems.

questions.question: What is Redux middleware and how does it work?
questions.answer: Middleware sits between dispatching an action and the moment it reaches the reducer, so it can log, handle async work, report crashes or perform other side effects without polluting reducers. Each middleware receives the store, wraps the next middleware, and must call next(action) to continue the chain; it can inspect, delay, modify or short-circuit the action along the way.

questions.question: What is a thunk, and how does createAsyncThunk simplify async logic?
questions.answer: A thunk is an action creator that returns a function instead of a plain object, which the redux-thunk middleware intercepts and invokes with dispatch/getState instead of passing to the reducer, enabling async or conditional dispatch logic. createAsyncThunk in Redux Toolkit wraps this pattern and automatically dispatches pending/fulfilled/rejected actions for a given async call, removing the boilerplate of manually tracking loading and error state.

questions.question: How do you avoid unnecessary re-renders with useSelector?
questions.answer: useSelector re-renders the component whenever the selected value is not reference-equal to the previous result on a state change, so returning a new object or array literal from the selector forces a re-render even when the underlying data has not changed. Select the narrowest primitive or memoized value a component actually needs, use a library like reselect (createSelector) for derived/computed data, or pass shallowEqual as the equality function when a shallow comparison is sufficient.
questions.code:
const name = useSelector(state => state.user.name);
const items = useSelector(selectFilteredItems, shallowEqual);

questions.question: What does it mean to normalize Redux state shape, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Normalization stores entities keyed by id, similar to a database table, instead of nesting duplicate copies of the same object throughout the state tree. It prevents update bugs caused by stale duplicated data, makes lookups by id O(1), and keeps reducers simpler since each entity has one source of truth. Redux Toolkit's createEntityAdapter provides normalized CRUD reducers and generated selectors so this pattern does not have to be hand-rolled.

questions.question: What is RTK Query, and when would you reach for it instead of hand-written thunks?
questions.answer: RTK Query is the data-fetching and caching layer built into Redux Toolkit. It generates hooks per endpoint and handles caching, request deduplication, background refetching and cache invalidation through tags, along with loading/error state, without hand-written reducers or thunks. I would use it for typical CRUD API interactions and reserve manual thunks for cases needing unusual side-effect orchestration that does not fit the fetch-and-cache model.

sections.title: 5. What Happens When You Enter a URL?

questions.question: Give me the complete interview answer.
questions.answer: When I enter a URL, the browser first parses it and checks applicable caches such as browser cache and DNS cache. It identifies the protocol and hostname. DNS resolution translates the hostname into an IP address. For HTTPS using HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, the browser establishes a TCP connection and performs a TLS handshake; HTTP/3 uses QUIC. The browser then sends an HTTP request. The request may pass through a CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy and web/application servers. The application may access databases or downstream services before generating the response. The browser receives the response and processes the returned resources. For HTML it builds the DOM; CSS is parsed into the CSSOM. Together they form the render tree. The browser calculates layout, paints pixels and composites layers. JavaScript can then modify the DOM or application state. With React/Next.js, the final behavior depends on whether the page is client-rendered, server-rendered or statically generated; React may hydrate server-rendered HTML to make it interactive.

questions.question: What is DNS?
questions.answer: DNS maps domain names to IP addresses. The browser/OS may already have a cached result. Otherwise a resolver can query DNS servers until it reaches an authoritative answer. DNS can also provide records used for routing and service configuration.

questions.question: TCP vs UDP?
questions.answer: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery with connection management and retransmission. UDP is connectionless and does not provide the same delivery guarantees. QUIC, used by HTTP/3, runs over UDP and provides reliability and encryption at the protocol level.

questions.question: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3?
questions.answer: HTTP/1.1 commonly uses one request stream per connection with persistent connections and can suffer from head-of-line effects at the application layer. HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexes streams over a connection. HTTP/3 uses HTTP semantics over QUIC, which runs over UDP and avoids TCP's transport-level head-of-line blocking between independent streams.

questions.question: What is TLS?
questions.answer: TLS provides encrypted communication, server authentication using certificates and integrity protection. HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS.

questions.question: What is CORS and preflight?
questions.answer: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can make cross-origin requests. For certain non-simple requests, the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking whether the actual request is allowed. The server responds with appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

questions.question: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage?
questions.answer: Cookies can be sent automatically with requests and can be HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. localStorage persists until explicitly cleared and is accessible to JavaScript. sessionStorage is scoped to a browser tab/session. For sensitive authentication credentials, storage choice should be based on the threat model; HttpOnly cookies can reduce direct JavaScript access to tokens.

questions.question: What is Node.js?
questions.answer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on V8. Its event-driven, non-blocking I/O architecture is well suited to APIs, real-time services and I/O-heavy applications. CPU-intensive synchronous JavaScript can block the event loop.

questions.question: What exactly happens with const app = express()?
questions.answer: express is a function exported by the Express framework. Calling it creates an Express application object. That object holds middleware and routing configuration and exposes methods such as use, get, post and listen. It does not itself start listening on a network port until app.listen is called.

questions.question: What happens when a request reaches Express?
questions.answer: The Node HTTP server receives the request and Express passes it through its middleware stack in order. Each middleware can inspect or modify the request/response, terminate the response, or call next(). If a matching route handler is reached, it executes and sends a response. Errors can be passed to error-handling middleware.

questions.question: What is middleware?
questions.answer: Middleware is a function that participates in the request-response pipeline. Typical middleware handles JSON parsing, authentication, logging, validation, rate limiting or error handling. Order is important.

questions.question: What is Node's event loop?
questions.answer: The event loop lets Node coordinate asynchronous I/O without blocking the JavaScript thread for every operation. Node delegates suitable work to the OS or internal facilities and later executes callbacks when results are ready. Long synchronous CPU work can block other requests.

questions.question: What can block Node.js?
questions.answer: Large synchronous loops, expensive JSON processing, cryptographic CPU work, synchronous filesystem operations and other CPU-heavy JavaScript can block the event loop. For CPU-heavy workloads, consider optimization, worker threads, separate services or other architectural approaches.

questions.question: What are streams?
questions.answer: Streams process data incrementally instead of loading the entire payload into memory at once. They are useful for large files, network data and pipelines.
questions.code:
const fs = require("fs");
fs.createReadStream("large.csv").pipe(res);

questions.question: How do you handle errors in Express?
questions.answer: Use consistent error handling. Route/service code can throw or pass errors, and a final error middleware can map known errors to appropriate status codes while logging unexpected failures without exposing sensitive internals.

questions.question: What is REST?
questions.answer: REST is an architectural style for resource-oriented APIs using HTTP semantics. Good REST APIs use clear resources, appropriate HTTP methods and status codes, predictable representations and stateless request handling.

questions.question: React vs Next.js?
questions.answer: React is a UI library. Next.js is a framework around React providing routing, server rendering options, Server Components, middleware, route handlers, caching and build optimizations.

questions.question: App Router vs Pages Router?
questions.answer: The App Router is the modern Next.js routing model built around layouts, nested routing and Server Components. The Pages Router is the older routing model and remains relevant for existing applications. For new development I generally prefer App Router when project requirements support it.

questions.question: Server Component vs Client Component?
questions.answer: Server Components run on the server and can keep server-only logic out of the browser bundle. Client Components are needed for browser interactivity, stateful hooks and browser APIs. I keep client boundaries as small as practical.

questions.question: What does 'use client' do?
questions.answer: It marks a module as a Client Component entry point in the App Router. Components in that boundary can use client-side hooks and browser APIs. It should not be added to every component by default.

questions.question: What is hydration?
questions.answer: Hydration attaches React's client behavior to server-rendered HTML. If server and client generate different initial output, hydration warnings or mismatches can occur.

questions.question: SSR vs CSR vs SSG?
questions.answer: SSR renders HTML on the server for a request. CSR renders primarily in the browser after JavaScript loads. SSG generates HTML ahead of time. The correct choice depends on freshness, SEO, personalization and performance requirements.

questions.question: What is middleware in Next.js?
questions.answer: Middleware can inspect incoming requests before they reach matched routes and perform redirects, rewrites or request-level checks such as authentication. It should remain lightweight.

questions.question: How would you migrate a React SPA to Next.js?
questions.answer: First inventory routing, authentication, API calls, state and browser-only dependencies. Then establish the Next.js routing/layout structure and migrate routes incrementally. Identify Client Components where browser APIs/hooks are needed and keep server-capable components on the server. Validate authentication, cookies, hydration and environment configuration during each stage rather than attempting a risky all-at-once rewrite.

questions.question: Authentication vs authorization?
questions.answer: Authentication establishes identity. Authorization determines permissions. A logged-in user may still be forbidden from approving a transaction.

questions.question: What is JWT?
questions.answer: A JWT is a signed token carrying claims. The server validates the signature and relevant claims. JWT is a token format, not a complete security architecture.

questions.question: Access token vs refresh token?
questions.answer: An access token is typically short-lived and used to access APIs. A refresh token is used to obtain a new access token and should have stronger protection and rotation/revocation controls.

questions.question: What is XSS?
questions.answer: Cross-site scripting occurs when attacker-controlled content is executed as script in another user's browser. Prevent it with proper output encoding, safe rendering, input handling, CSP and avoiding unsafe HTML injection.

questions.question: What is CSRF?
questions.answer: Cross-site request forgery tricks a user's browser into sending an authenticated request to a site. SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and appropriate request validation are common defenses depending on architecture.

questions.question: What is rate limiting?
questions.answer: Rate limiting restricts how frequently a client can call an API. It protects availability and reduces abuse such as brute-force attempts or accidental request storms.

questions.question: Design a large ERP frontend.
questions.answer:
I would organize around business domains rather than one giant technical folder. Each module owns its screens, components, hooks, state and services. Shared UI components and utilities remain centralized. API communication is separated from presentation, authentication and permissions are cross-cutting concerns, and global state is limited to data that genuinely needs shared ownership. The architecture should make it possible for multiple teams to work independently without duplicating core components.
src/
  modules/
    sales/
    procurement/
    workOrders/
  components/
  hooks/
  services/
  store/
  utils/
  styles/

questions.question: Design an API-driven dynamic form.
questions.answer: Define a schema for field metadata: field type, label, value mapping, validation, options, visibility, dependencies and submission behavior. A generic form renderer consumes the schema, while extension points handle specialized fields. Business rules should not become hard-coded into the generic renderer. This allows new transaction types to be introduced through configuration plus limited custom logic.

questions.question: How should business logic be separated?
questions.answer: Keep presentation logic in components, reusable stateful behavior in hooks, API communication in service layers, shared state in Redux or another appropriate state mechanism, and pure transformations in utilities/domain functions. The exact boundaries depend on the application, but the goal is testability and clear ownership rather than a rigid folder structure.

questions.question: How would you design authentication?
questions.answer: Start with the threat model and identity provider. Keep authentication state consistent across server and client boundaries. Protect sensitive credentials appropriately, enforce authorization on the server/API rather than relying only on hidden UI, and handle token expiration, logout and refresh/revocation. In Next.js, middleware can assist with request-level redirects/checks, while actual authorization must be enforced by protected server/API logic.

questions.question: How do you investigate a slow React page?
questions.answer: Measure first: React Profiler for component renders, browser Performance panel for CPU/layout/paint, Network for API/bundle timing and Memory for leaks or excessive allocations. Then classify the bottleneck and fix the root cause.

questions.question: How do you handle 100K records in React?
questions.answer: Do not render all records at once. Use pagination or virtualization, server-side filtering/sorting where appropriate, efficient selectors, stable row rendering and incremental data loading. For very large datasets, move expensive processing closer to the data source rather than doing everything in the browser.

questions.question: How would you handle 80K+ Mapbox points?
questions.answer: Filter by viewport first, then reduce data according to zoom and density, remove redundant points, minimize object/GeoJSON creation and avoid rendering points that cannot be visually distinguished at the current zoom. Profile CPU and memory and validate responsiveness after each change.

questions.question: What is virtualization?
questions.answer: Virtualization renders only the visible portion of a large list or grid instead of creating DOM nodes for every item. It can dramatically reduce rendering and layout cost.

questions.question: What is memoization?
questions.answer: Memoization caches a result so repeated computation can be avoided when inputs have not changed. It can help performance but adds memory and comparison overhead, so it should be used where it provides measurable benefit.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: I am a Senior Software Engineer with 14+ years of experience, with my recent career focused on frontend and enterprise web application development. My strongest areas are React.js, JavaScript, Next.js, Redux, API integration and frontend performance. In my current role I work on enterprise security and safety software, including reusable business modules, complex workflows and Mapbox-based large-data visualization. I enjoy solving difficult frontend problems, improving architecture and taking ownership from requirement through production delivery. I am now looking for a role with broader technical challenges and continued growth as a senior frontend engineer.

questions.question: Why are you looking for a change?
questions.answer: I have had a valuable experience in my current organization and have taken ownership of technically challenging areas. At this stage I am looking for broader technical challenges, stronger opportunities to contribute to architecture and modern frontend engineering, and continued growth in React, Next.js and enterprise application design. I want the move to be about the next level of responsibility.

questions.question: Why should we hire you?
questions.answer: I bring a combination of long-term engineering experience and recent hands-on frontend expertise. I can contribute at implementation level with React and JavaScript, while also reasoning about architecture, performance, APIs and business workflows. I understand ownership, communication, code quality and production stability.

questions.question: What is your biggest strength?
questions.answer: My strength is combining hands-on implementation with problem solving and ownership. I can work at component level, but I also think about state boundaries, APIs, performance, maintainability and business requirements.

questions.question: What is your weakness?
questions.answer: Earlier in my career I sometimes spent too much time making an implementation perfect before sharing it. With experience I learned to validate direction earlier, get feedback sooner and improve iteratively. That has made me more efficient without lowering quality.

questions.question: Tell me about a production issue.
questions.answer: Use a real example. Structure it as: problem, impact, investigation, root cause, fix, validation and prevention. Do not blame another team. Explain what you learned and what you changed to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: Tell me about a conflict.
questions.answer: Describe a technical disagreement, explain both viewpoints, show how you used evidence or a small proof of concept to decide, and finish with the outcome. The goal is to demonstrate professional collaboration rather than winning an argument.

questions.question: Salary expectation?
questions.answer: I am looking for a compensation package aligned with the role, responsibilities, market and my experience. I am open to discussing the overall package once I understand the role and expectations in detail. If the company requires a number early, give a researched range rather than an unnecessarily low single number.

parts.title: PART XIII — EXTENDED TOPICS & QUESTION BANK

questions.question: Why use TypeScript in a large frontend application?
questions.answer: TypeScript adds static type checking, better refactoring support, clearer contracts and safer API/component boundaries. In a large enterprise application, the biggest benefit is reducing ambiguity between modules and catching incompatible changes before runtime.

questions.question: interface vs type?
questions.answer: Both can describe object shapes. Interfaces are particularly useful for extendable object contracts and declaration merging; type aliases are more flexible for unions, intersections, tuples and mapped types. In a project I would follow the team's conventions rather than treating one as universally superior.

questions.question: any vs unknown?
questions.answer: any disables most type checking and should be used sparingly. unknown is type-safe: you must narrow it before using it as a specific type. For external API data, unknown is generally safer than any.

questions.question: What are generics?
questions.answer: Generics allow reusable code to preserve type information instead of falling back to broad types. They are especially useful for reusable API responses, tables, hooks and utility functions.

questions.question: What is a union vs intersection?
questions.answer: A union A | B means a value can be A or B and must be narrowed before using type-specific members. An intersection A & B combines requirements from both types.

questions.question: How would you type an API response?
questions.answer: I would define a reusable response contract and domain-specific payload types, while remembering that TypeScript types disappear at runtime. External data should still be validated when runtime safety matters.

questions.question: What is type narrowing?
questions.answer: Type narrowing uses checks such as typeof, in, instanceof or custom type guards to reduce a broad type to a more specific type within a code path.

questions.question: Why are Server Components useful?
questions.answer: They allow rendering and data access to happen on the server and can reduce the JavaScript sent to the browser. The key architectural idea is the server/client network boundary, not simply 'server is faster'.

questions.question: What should stay on the server in Next.js?
questions.answer: Secrets, server-only credentials, privileged data access and work that does not require browser interactivity are strong candidates. The client should receive only what it needs.

questions.question: How do you decide where a client boundary belongs?
questions.answer: Start with server-capable components. Introduce a Client Component where you need state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs. Keep the client boundary as small as practical so unnecessary code is not shipped to the browser.

questions.question: How would you debug a hydration mismatch?
questions.answer: Identify what differs between server and client output. Common causes include browser-only APIs during render, non-deterministic values such as Date/randomness, conditional rendering based on client state, and mismatched data. Move client-only behavior behind an appropriate client boundary/effect or make the initial render deterministic.

questions.question: How would you design caching in a Next.js application?
questions.answer: Start by classifying data: static, revalidated, user-specific or always-fresh. Then choose the appropriate framework and API caching behavior. Avoid caching personalized data accidentally and make invalidation rules explicit.

sections.title: D. Accessibility — Frequently Expected at Senior Level

questions.question: What is accessibility in frontend development?
questions.answer: Accessibility means designing the application so people with different abilities can use it, including keyboard users and users of assistive technologies. It includes semantic HTML, focus management, labels, contrast, keyboard interaction and appropriate ARIA when native HTML is insufficient.

questions.question: Why prefer semantic HTML over ARIA?
questions.answer: Native HTML elements already carry useful semantics and browser behavior. ARIA should enhance semantics when necessary, not replace correct native elements unnecessarily.

questions.question: How would you make a modal accessible?
questions.answer: Manage focus when it opens, provide an accessible name, keep keyboard interaction predictable, support Escape where appropriate, prevent focus from escaping the modal, and restore focus to the triggering element when it closes.

questions.question: How do you test keyboard accessibility?
questions.answer: Navigate the complete workflow without a mouse: Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and relevant arrow keys. Check visible focus, logical order, interactive control semantics and whether dialogs/menus trap or restore focus correctly.

questions.question: Unit vs integration vs E2E testing?
questions.answer: Unit tests validate small isolated logic. Integration tests verify multiple pieces working together, such as a component with state and API boundaries. E2E tests validate complete user workflows in a real browser-like environment. A balanced suite uses each where it provides the most confidence.

questions.question: What should you test in a React component?
questions.answer: Test user-visible behavior and important state transitions rather than implementation details. For example, submit a form, validate an error, mock the API response and verify what the user sees.

questions.question: What makes a test brittle?
questions.answer: Tests become brittle when they depend heavily on internal implementation, exact DOM structure or incidental timing rather than behavior. Prefer stable user-facing queries and deterministic test data.

questions.question: What would you test for an API-driven form engine?
questions.answer: Schema parsing, field rendering, validation, conditional visibility, dependencies, submission mapping, API failure handling, permission rules and representative transaction configurations.

sections.title: F. Web Performance & Core Web Vitals

questions.question: What are Core Web Vitals?
questions.answer: They are user-experience performance metrics used by the web platform. Important current metrics include LCP for loading performance, INP for interaction responsiveness and CLS for visual stability. In an interview, focus on how you measure and improve them rather than memorizing thresholds.

questions.question: How would you improve LCP?
questions.answer: Optimize the critical rendering path: reduce server response time, prioritize the main content resource, optimize images/fonts, reduce render-blocking work and avoid shipping unnecessary JavaScript before the main content is usable.

questions.question: How would you improve INP?
questions.answer: Find long-running main-thread tasks, reduce JavaScript work, break up expensive processing, avoid unnecessary renders and use appropriate scheduling/concurrency techniques for non-urgent updates.

questions.question: How would you investigate a memory leak?
questions.answer: Use browser memory tools and heap snapshots, reproduce the issue, compare retained objects over time and look for unremoved event listeners, timers, subscriptions, detached DOM trees or retained closures. Fix the ownership/cleanup problem and retest.

questions.question: How do you protect a React application from XSS?
questions.answer: Avoid unsafe HTML injection, encode untrusted output, sanitize when HTML is genuinely required, use Content Security Policy where appropriate and keep authentication secrets out of places where untrusted scripts can easily access them.

questions.question: Why is hiding a button not authorization?
questions.answer: UI visibility is only a user-experience control. A malicious client can call an API directly. The backend/API must enforce the permission regardless of what the UI displays.

questions.question: How should secrets be handled in a Next.js application?
questions.answer: Server secrets must remain server-side and must not be exposed through public environment variables or client bundles. Anything intentionally exposed to the browser should be treated as public.

questions.question: How do you debug a production frontend issue?
questions.answer: First reproduce or characterize the failure. Check logs, monitoring, browser errors, network failures and affected versions. Determine whether it is client, API, data or deployment related. Apply the smallest safe fix, validate it, monitor the result and document the root cause and prevention.

questions.question: What should frontend observability include?
questions.answer: Error tracking, structured application events where useful, performance metrics, API timing, release/version information and enough context to correlate failures without collecting unnecessary sensitive data.

questions.question: How do you handle a production incident?
questions.answer: Stabilize first, communicate impact, identify scope, mitigate safely, investigate root cause, deploy/rollback, verify recovery and then conduct a blameless post-incident review with prevention actions.

questions.question: What should a frontend CI pipeline do?
questions.answer: Install reproducibly, lint, type-check, run unit/integration tests, build the application and perform security/quality checks appropriate to the project. Deployment should promote a tested artifact rather than rebuilding unpredictably in production.

questions.question: Rebase vs merge?
questions.answer: Both integrate history. Rebase creates a linear history by replaying commits on a new base, while merge creates a merge commit that preserves branch history. The choice should follow team conventions and avoid rewriting shared history unexpectedly.

questions.question: How would you safely release a frontend change?
questions.answer: Use CI validation, environment-specific configuration, feature flags or incremental rollout when appropriate, monitor errors/performance after release and keep a rollback path.

sections.title: J. Frontend System Design — Modern Questions

questions.question: Design a large data table for an ERP.
questions.answer: Use server-side filtering/sorting/pagination for large datasets, virtualization for visible rows, stable column definitions, debounced search, accessible keyboard interaction and careful state ownership. Do not load or render hundreds of thousands of rows unnecessarily.

questions.question: Design a notification system.
questions.answer: Separate event generation from delivery and presentation. The frontend should consume a stable API/stream, maintain unread/read state, handle reconnection and avoid duplicate notifications. The backend remains authoritative for persistence.

questions.question: Design a file upload workflow.
questions.answer: Validate type/size, show progress, support cancellation/retry when useful, upload directly to object storage when appropriate, avoid loading large files entirely into memory, and make server-side validation authoritative.

questions.question: Design a scalable frontend for multiple teams.
questions.answer: Define module boundaries, shared design-system components, clear API contracts, lint/type/test standards, ownership rules and CI gates. Avoid a shared component library becoming a bottleneck by defining contribution and versioning practices.

questions.question: How would you migrate a legacy React application safely?
questions.answer: Inventory dependencies and risk areas, establish tests around critical workflows, introduce the new architecture incrementally, migrate one domain at a time, keep observability in place and avoid combining framework migration with unrelated business changes.

questions.question: How do you mentor a developer?
questions.answer: Understand their current level, give context rather than only fixes, review their reasoning, pair on difficult problems and gradually increase ownership. The goal is independent decision-making rather than dependency on the mentor.

questions.question: How do you handle disagreement about architecture?
questions.answer: Clarify the actual problem and constraints, compare alternatives using evidence, prototype if needed, document trade-offs and make a decision aligned with product and engineering priorities. Once decided, commit to the team direction.

questions.question: How do you prioritize technical debt?
questions.answer: Rank it by user impact, production risk, developer productivity and cost of delay. Technical debt that blocks delivery or causes recurring incidents should receive higher priority than cosmetic refactoring.

questions.question: What makes someone senior?
questions.answer: Not simply years of experience. A senior engineer can reason about trade-offs, own outcomes, debug ambiguous problems, communicate clearly, improve systems rather than only tickets, and help other engineers make better decisions.

sections.title: N1. TypeScript Fundamentals and Practical Typing

questions.question: Why is TypeScript important in a large React/Next.js application?
questions.answer:
Interview answer: TypeScript gives us compile-time feedback about contracts between components, APIs and modules. In a large codebase, its biggest value is safer refactoring and clearer boundaries. It does not replace runtime validation because external data can still be invalid.
Senior point: Use types to model the domain, not merely to remove red underlines. Prefer precise types at public boundaries and allow inference inside small functions.

questions.question: interface vs type — what should I say in an interview?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Both can describe object shapes. interface is naturally suited to extendable object contracts and supports declaration merging. type is more flexible for unions, intersections, tuples and mapped/conditional types. I follow team conventions rather than treating one as universally better.

questions.question: any vs unknown vs never?
questions.answer: Interview answer: any effectively opts out of type checking. unknown represents a value whose type is not yet known and forces narrowing before use. never represents something that cannot occur, such as an exhaustive switch branch or a function that always throws.

questions.question: What are generics and where would you use them?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Generics let reusable code preserve the caller's type information. They are useful for reusable tables, API responses, hooks, repositories and form utilities.

questions.question: How do you type dynamic ERP forms?
questions.answer: Interview answer: I model common field properties with a base type and use discriminated unions for field-specific configuration. That lets TypeScript narrow the configuration safely based on field type.

questions.question: Why doesn't TypeScript guarantee API data is valid?
questions.answer:
Interview answer: TypeScript types disappear at runtime. If an API returns malformed data, a type assertion does not validate it. At trust boundaries I validate important external data with runtime checks or a schema-validation library.
Common mistake: Writing `const data = await res.json() as User` and assuming the server response has been validated.

sections.title: N4. Server/Client Boundaries in Modern Next.js

questions.question: What is the default component model in the App Router?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Pages and layouts are Server Components by default. I add a Client Component boundary only where I need state, event handlers, effects, custom client hooks or browser-only APIs.

questions.question: Why keep the client boundary small?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Everything imported below a 'use client' boundary becomes part of the client module graph. Smaller client boundaries reduce browser JavaScript and keep server-only logic, data access and secrets away from the client.

questions.question: When should data fetching happen on the server?
questions.answer: Interview answer: When data can be fetched securely near its source and does not require browser-only context, server fetching can reduce client waterfalls and keep credentials/server logic private. Client fetching remains appropriate for highly interactive or browser-dependent workflows.

questions.question: What causes hydration mismatch?
questions.answer: Interview answer: The initial client render does not match the server-rendered HTML. Typical causes are Date/random values, reading window/localStorage during render, locale differences, invalid HTML nesting or rendering different content based on client-only state.

questions.question: Can a Server Component be visually nested inside a Client Component?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Yes. A Server Component can be passed as children or another serializable composition slot to a Client Component. The important distinction is module ownership and where the components are rendered, not simply what visually contains what.

questions.question: What does accessibility mean for a frontend engineer?
questions.answer: Interview answer: It means users can understand and operate the application with different input methods and assistive technologies. I start with semantic HTML, keyboard access, focus management, labels and understandable error states, then use ARIA only where native semantics are insufficient.

questions.question: Why is semantic HTML important?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Native elements already provide semantics, keyboard behavior and accessibility mappings. A button should normally be a `<button>`, not a clickable `<div>` with many attributes recreated manually.

questions.question: How do you make a modal/dialog accessible?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Give it an accessible name, move focus into it when opened, keep keyboard focus within the dialog while active, support expected keyboard behavior such as Escape where appropriate, and restore focus to the trigger when it closes.

questions.question: What should an accessible form do?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Every control needs a programmatically associated label. Validation messages should identify the field and problem, required state should be conveyed semantically, focus should move predictably on errors, and the form must be usable without a mouse.

questions.question: What is your quick accessibility test before release?
questions.answer: Interview answer: I try the critical workflow using only the keyboard, check visible focus order, labels, headings, form errors and dialog behavior, then use automated tooling as an additional check—not as the only accessibility test.

sections.title: N6. Testing Strategy and Testable Architecture

questions.question: What is your testing strategy for a senior frontend project?
questions.answer: Interview answer: I use a risk-based test pyramid: unit tests for pure logic, integration/component tests for important UI behavior and boundaries, and a smaller number of E2E tests for critical user journeys. I optimize for confidence rather than maximum test count.

questions.question: What should a React component test focus on?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Observable user behavior: what the user sees, clicks, types and what happens after API success or failure. Tests coupled to internal state variables or exact implementation structure are more brittle.

questions.question: How would you test an API-driven form engine?
questions.answer: Interview answer: I would test schema-to-field rendering, validation, conditional visibility, dependencies, option loading, permissions, submission mapping, error states and representative complex transaction schemas.

questions.question: What should be mocked?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Mock unstable or external boundaries such as network requests, time or third-party integrations when needed. Avoid mocking the component's own implementation so heavily that the test stops representing real behavior.

questions.question: What makes frontend code testable?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Clear separation of pure transformations, API boundaries and UI behavior. Dependency injection or replaceable service boundaries help where appropriate. Components with excessive hidden global dependencies are harder to test and reason about.

sections.title: N7. Core Web Vitals and Real-User Performance

questions.question: What are Core Web Vitals?
questions.answer: Interview answer: They are user-centric web performance metrics. For interviews I focus on LCP for loading experience, INP for interaction responsiveness and CLS for visual stability, plus how I would measure and improve them.

questions.question: How would you improve LCP?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Identify the LCP element, then reduce server/network delay and render-blocking work. Prioritize the hero resource, optimize images/fonts, reduce unnecessary client JavaScript and avoid delaying important content behind client-only fetching.

questions.question: How would you improve INP?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Find long main-thread tasks around user interactions. Reduce JavaScript work, split heavy computation, reduce React rendering, virtualize large lists, avoid synchronous work in handlers and schedule non-urgent updates appropriately.

questions.question: How would you improve CLS?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Reserve dimensions for images and dynamic content, avoid inserting content above existing content unexpectedly, manage fonts carefully and keep animations/layout changes from shifting surrounding elements.

questions.question: Lab performance vs real-user performance?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Lab tools give controlled, repeatable diagnostics. Real-user monitoring shows what actual users experience across devices, networks and data sizes. I use both: lab tools to debug and RUM to prioritize and validate production impact.

sections.title: N8. Frontend Security and Server-Side Authorization

questions.question: What security responsibilities does a frontend engineer have?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Prevent unsafe rendering, protect sensitive data from accidental exposure, use secure authentication flows, avoid leaking secrets into client bundles, validate assumptions at trust boundaries and never treat UI restrictions as authorization.

questions.question: Why is hiding a button not authorization?
questions.answer: Interview answer: The browser is controlled by the user. They can modify JavaScript or call the API directly. The UI can hide actions for usability, but the API/server must enforce permission for every protected operation.

questions.question: How do you reduce XSS risk?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Use framework-safe rendering, avoid dangerously injecting HTML, sanitize unavoidable rich HTML, validate URLs and external content, consider CSP, and keep dependencies patched. Never assume input validation alone is enough.

questions.question: What is CSRF and when does it matter?
questions.answer: Interview answer: CSRF abuses a browser's automatic credential sending, commonly with cookie-based authentication, to make an unwanted request. Defenses can include SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens and origin/request validation depending on the architecture.

questions.question: Where should Next.js secrets live?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Secrets must remain in server-only environment/configuration and server code. Anything intentionally exposed to the client bundle must be treated as public. I also avoid passing sensitive server data unnecessarily into Client Component props.

questions.question: What does frontend observability include?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Error tracking, performance metrics, API timing/failures, release/version context and meaningful application events. The objective is to answer: what failed, for whom, in which release, under what conditions and how often?

questions.question: How do you debug a production-only issue?
questions.answer: Interview answer: First define the affected users, release, browser, route and data conditions. Check client errors, network traces, backend logs and deployment changes. Reproduce with production-like data, isolate the layer, apply the smallest safe fix, then monitor after release.

questions.question: How would you investigate a memory leak?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Reproduce the growth, take heap snapshots over time, inspect retained objects and detached DOM nodes, then look for listeners, timers, subscriptions, caches or closures that keep references alive after the UI should release them.

questions.question: How should you handle a production incident?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Stabilize service first, communicate impact, mitigate or roll back, identify root cause, validate recovery and then document prevention actions. During the incident I prioritize user impact and safe recovery over perfect diagnosis.

questions.question: What should a frontend CI pipeline contain?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Reproducible dependency installation, linting, type checking, tests, a production build and appropriate security/quality checks. The same tested artifact should ideally be promoted through environments rather than rebuilt differently for production.

questions.question: What is your safe release strategy?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Use automated checks, environment-specific configuration, feature flags or staged rollout for risky changes, observability after deployment and a clear rollback path.

questions.question: What is the role of feature flags?
questions.answer: Interview answer: They separate code deployment from feature exposure. They can enable gradual rollout and fast disablement, but stale flags create complexity, so they need ownership and cleanup.

questions.question: Merge vs rebase?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Merge preserves branch topology with a merge commit. Rebase replays commits on a new base and creates a linear history. I follow team policy and avoid rewriting commits that others already depend on.

questions.question: How do you prevent environment-specific bugs?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Keep configuration explicit, validate required environment variables, avoid environment-only manual steps, keep builds reproducible and test production-like behavior before release. Configuration is part of the application contract.

sections.title: N11. Frontend System Design and Machine-Coding

questions.question: How should you approach a frontend system-design interview?
questions.answer: Interview answer: I start with requirements and scale, identify users and critical flows, define domain/component boundaries, data ownership, API contracts, state strategy, performance, security, accessibility, failure states, observability and deployment. Then I discuss trade-offs rather than jumping directly into a folder structure.

questions.question: Design a large ERP transaction screen.
questions.answer: Interview answer: I would separate transaction metadata, schema/configuration, form state, lookups, permissions and submission workflow. Shared field components belong in a design/form system; transaction-specific rules remain within the domain. Large lookups should use server-side search or pagination rather than loading everything.

questions.question: Design a table with 100K+ rows.
questions.answer: Interview answer: Do not load and render 100K DOM rows. Use server-side pagination/filtering/sorting where possible, virtualization for the visible rows, debounced search, stable row identity and cancellation for stale requests. Preserve filters in URL/state when it improves workflow.

questions.question: Design an autocomplete with millions of records.
questions.answer: Interview answer: Use server-side search with a minimum query length, debounce, request cancellation/stale-response protection, limited result size, caching of useful recent queries and keyboard-accessible selection. Do not download the complete dataset.

questions.question: What do interviewers expect in machine coding?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Working behavior first, then clean component boundaries, readable state flow, edge cases, accessibility, error/loading states and reasonable tests. I narrate important decisions but avoid over-engineering a small exercise.

questions.question: How would you build a reusable modal component?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Define a small API, render through a portal if needed, manage focus, Escape/backdrop behavior, scroll locking and accessibility. Keep business-specific content outside the generic modal.

questions.question: How would you build infinite scrolling?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Use cursor/page-based API pagination, an IntersectionObserver sentinel, loading/error/end states, deduplication and protection from duplicate requests. For very long feeds, combine it with virtualization so DOM size does not grow indefinitely.

questions.question: How do you handle race conditions in search?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Debounce reduces request volume, but it does not guarantee response order. I cancel previous requests with AbortController or track request identity so an older response cannot overwrite newer results.

questions.question: Design a frontend notification architecture.
questions.answer: Interview answer: Keep the backend authoritative for persisted notifications. The frontend consumes an API or real-time channel, normalizes incoming events, deduplicates them, manages unread state, handles reconnect/backoff and presents notifications through a centralized UI layer.

questions.question: What is the most important senior-level trade-off in frontend architecture?
questions.answer: Interview answer: Avoid optimizing for theoretical elegance at the expense of delivery and maintainability. I choose the simplest architecture that meets current scale and leaves clear extension points. I make complexity earn its place.

questions.question: What are JavaScript data types?
questions.answer: Primitive types are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Objects include arrays, functions, dates, maps and sets.

questions.question: Why does typeof null return object?
questions.answer: It is a historical JavaScript compatibility quirk. null is still a primitive.

questions.question: == vs ===?
questions.answer: === compares without type coercion. == applies coercion rules. I normally prefer === in application code for predictability.

questions.question: Truthy vs falsy?
questions.answer: Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, empty string, null, undefined and NaN. Objects and arrays are truthy, even when empty.

questions.question: null vs undefined?
questions.answer: undefined commonly represents missing/uninitialized values; null is an explicit absence marker. Teams should use a consistent convention.

questions.question: What is NaN?
questions.answer: NaN is a special numeric value representing an invalid numeric result. It is not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN to test it.

questions.question: What is Object.is?
questions.answer: It uses SameValue semantics: NaN equals itself and +0 differs from -0.

questions.question: Is JavaScript pass-by-reference?
questions.answer: Technically JavaScript passes arguments by value. For objects, the copied value is a reference to the same object. Saying 'objects are passed by reference' is a useful shorthand but not technically precise.

questions.question: Optional chaining?
questions.answer: ?. safely stops a property/call chain when the preceding value is nullish and returns undefined.

questions.question: Nullish coalescing?
questions.answer: ?? uses the fallback only for null or undefined, unlike || which also treats 0, false and '' as falsy.

questions.question: Short-circuit evaluation?
questions.answer: && stops on falsy; || stops on truthy; ?? stops when the left side is not nullish.

questions.question: Higher-order function?
questions.answer: A function that accepts functions, returns a function, or both. map/filter and function factories are examples.

questions.question: Currying?
questions.answer: Converting a multi-argument function into a sequence of single-argument functions.

questions.question: Partial application?
questions.answer: Fixing some arguments now and returning a function that accepts the rest.

questions.question: Function composition?
questions.answer: Combining small functions so one output becomes another function's input.

questions.question: IIFE?
questions.answer: Immediately Invoked Function Expression. Historically used to create private scope before modern modules and block scope.

questions.question: ES Modules vs CommonJS?
questions.answer: ESM uses import/export and is the standard module system. CommonJS uses require/module.exports and remains common in Node projects.

questions.question: Tree shaking?
questions.answer: Removing statically unreachable exports from a production bundle. It works best with statically analyzable ES modules.

questions.question: Dynamic import?
questions.answer: import() loads a module asynchronously and returns a Promise; it is useful for code splitting.

questions.question: Strict mode?
questions.answer: It enables stricter JavaScript semantics and catches unsafe patterns. ES modules are implicitly strict.

questions.question: Garbage collection?
questions.answer: The engine reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable. Retained references can prevent collection.

questions.question: Common frontend memory leaks?
questions.answer: Unremoved listeners, timers, subscriptions, retained closures, global caches and detached DOM nodes.

questions.question: WeakMap?
questions.answer: A key-value structure with object keys that does not keep those keys alive for garbage collection.

questions.question: Map vs Object?
questions.answer: Map is designed for key-value collections and arbitrary key types; Object is often better for fixed record-like structures.

questions.question: Set vs Array?
questions.answer: Set stores unique values and is useful for membership checks; Array is ordered and indexable.

questions.question: Event delegation?
questions.answer: Attach one listener to a common ancestor and use bubbling to handle child events. It works well for dynamic lists.

questions.question: Bubbling vs capturing?
questions.answer: Events travel through capture toward the target, reach the target, then bubble back. addEventListener can opt into capture.

questions.question: stopPropagation vs preventDefault?
questions.answer: stopPropagation affects event propagation. preventDefault cancels a browser default action when possible.

questions.question: AbortController?
questions.answer: Provides a signal used to cancel operations such as fetch.

questions.question: Why cancel stale requests?
questions.answer: It saves work and prevents older responses from overwriting newer UI state.

questions.question: Race condition?
questions.answer: Asynchronous operations finish in an unexpected order and the application incorrectly assumes the start order equals the completion order.

questions.question: JSON cloning limitations?
questions.answer: Functions, undefined, symbols and special object types are not faithfully represented; circular structures fail.

questions.question: structuredClone?
questions.answer: A modern structured cloning API that handles many built-in values and circular references better than JSON cloning, with supported-type limitations.

questions.question: Generator?
questions.answer: A function using yield that can pause and resume and exposes an iterator.

questions.question: Symbol?
questions.answer: A unique primitive often used for unique object keys and language protocols.

questions.question: BigInt?
questions.answer: An integer type for values beyond Number's safe integer range. Do not mix BigInt and Number directly in arithmetic.

questions.question: Lexical this in arrow functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions capture this from the surrounding lexical scope instead of creating their own dynamic this.

questions.question: Why can extracted methods lose this?
questions.answer: A normal function gets this from its call site. Extracting obj.method into a variable removes the object receiver unless it is bound.

questions.question: Debounce vs throttle?
questions.answer: Debounce waits for inactivity; throttle limits execution frequency.

questions.question: What is immutability?
questions.answer: Create a new value rather than mutating the existing one. It makes state changes easier to detect and reason about, especially in React/Redux.

questions.question: Predict the output.
questions.answer: Expected: 1, 5, 3, 4, 2. Synchronous code completes first, then microtasks in queue order, then the timer task.

questions.question: Predict the output.
questions.answer: regular() receives user as its this value. The arrow function does not bind this to user; it captures lexical this from the surrounding scope.

questions.question: Predict the output.
What is semantic HTML?
questions.answer: Use elements according to meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, button, form, footer and so on. It improves accessibility, maintainability and browser behavior.

questions.question: div vs section?
questions.answer: div has no semantic meaning; section represents a thematic grouping and normally has an identifiable purpose/heading.

questions.question: article vs section?
questions.answer: article is suitable for self-contained/distributable content; section groups related content.

questions.question: main vs div?
questions.answer: main identifies the primary content of the document and creates a useful accessibility landmark.

questions.question: What is the DOM?
questions.answer: The browser's object representation of the document, which scripts and browser APIs can inspect and manipulate.

questions.question: What is the viewport meta tag?
questions.answer: It controls the mobile layout viewport and scaling. A common responsive setting uses width=device-width.

questions.question: Why is alt text important?
questions.answer: It provides a text alternative for meaningful images. Decorative images can use empty alt text.

questions.question: img vs background-image?
questions.answer: Use img for content images needing semantics/alt text; background-image is generally for decoration.

questions.question: label vs placeholder?
questions.answer: A label identifies a control and should remain available. Placeholder is only a hint.

questions.question: button vs anchor?
questions.answer: button performs an action; anchor navigates. Using the semantic element gives correct keyboard and accessibility behavior.

questions.question: GET vs POST form?
questions.answer: GET suits retrieval/search and URL-addressable queries; POST is generally used for state-changing submissions.

questions.question: What is progressive enhancement?
questions.answer: Build a functional baseline using platform capabilities, then enhance with CSS and JavaScript.

questions.question: What is ARIA?
questions.answer: Accessibility semantics/states used when native HTML cannot express the required behavior. Prefer native semantics first.

questions.question: Why lang attribute?
questions.answer: It identifies document language for assistive technology and text processing.

questions.question: async vs defer?
questions.answer: Both avoid the blocking behavior of classic synchronous scripts. defer preserves order and runs after parsing; async runs when ready and does not guarantee order.

questions.question: Why can script loading affect performance?
questions.answer: Synchronous scripts can block parsing/execution. Deferring non-critical code improves initial loading.

questions.question: What is a form's accessible error strategy?
questions.answer: Associate errors with fields, identify the problem clearly, preserve keyboard access and provide predictable focus behavior.

questions.question: What are landmark elements?
questions.answer: Semantic regions such as header, nav, main, aside and footer help assistive technology navigate page structure.

questions.question: Why should heading levels be meaningful?
questions.answer: Headings communicate document structure. Do not choose heading levels merely for font size; style them with CSS.
questions.code: Orders

questions.question: Explain the box model.
questions.answer: Content, padding, border and margin. box-sizing controls whether declared dimensions include padding/border; border-box is often easier to reason about.

questions.question: What is margin collapse?
questions.answer: Certain vertical margins in normal flow can collapse into one margin, which can produce surprising spacing.

questions.question: Explain specificity.
questions.answer: Specificity ranks competing selectors after cascade origin/layer considerations. IDs outrank classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, which outrank element selectors.

questions.question: What is the cascade?
questions.answer: The browser resolves competing declarations using origin/importance, cascade layers, specificity and source order.

questions.question: What is inheritance?
questions.answer: Some properties naturally inherit from ancestors, such as color and font properties; others do not.

questions.question: Flexbox?
questions.answer: A one-dimensional layout system for arranging items along a main axis with cross-axis alignment.

questions.question: Grid?
questions.answer: A two-dimensional layout system for rows and columns.

questions.question: Flex vs Grid?
questions.answer: Use Flex for primarily one-dimensional layouts and Grid when rows and columns both matter.

questions.question: justify-content vs align-items?
questions.answer: They control distribution/alignment along different axes depending on the layout.

questions.question: What is flex:1?
questions.answer: Commonly expands to grow/shrink with a zero basis, allowing siblings to share available space.

questions.question: position modes?
questions.answer: relative offsets from normal position; absolute leaves normal flow and uses a containing block; fixed is viewport-oriented; sticky sticks within scroll constraints.

questions.question: What creates a stacking context?
questions.answer: Properties such as positioned z-index elements, opacity, transforms and isolation can create independent stacking contexts.

questions.question: Why does z-index not work?
questions.answer: The element may be trapped in another stacking context. Increasing z-index inside the wrong context cannot cross that context.

questions.question: CSS specificity hell?
questions.answer: Overly specific selectors make overrides difficult. Prefer predictable scoping, low specificity and design tokens.

questions.question: CSS custom properties?
questions.answer: Runtime variables such as --color-primary that participate in the cascade and are excellent for theming.

questions.question: Sass variables vs CSS variables?
questions.answer: Sass variables are compile-time; CSS custom properties exist at runtime and can change through the cascade.

questions.question: Responsive design?
questions.answer: Adapt layout and interaction to viewport/container size using flexible units, media/container queries and responsive assets.

questions.question: Media vs container queries?
questions.answer: Media queries react to viewport/device conditions; container queries react to the size of a component's container.

questions.question: Mobile-first CSS?
questions.answer: Start with the base/small-screen layout and progressively enhance for larger conditions.

questions.question: BEM?
questions.answer: Block Element Modifier naming methodology that makes class relationships explicit.

questions.question: CSS Modules?
questions.answer: Build-time scoping of class names to reduce global collisions.

questions.question: CSS-in-JS pros/cons?
questions.answer: Can colocate styling and dynamic logic, but may add runtime/build complexity and ecosystem trade-offs.

questions.question: Utility-first CSS?
questions.answer: Compose small utility classes for styling. It improves consistency but needs conventions to keep markup readable.

questions.question: SCSS architecture?
questions.answer: Separate tokens, mixins, base styles, component styles and utilities; avoid deep nesting and global coupling.

questions.question: Dark mode?
questions.answer: Use semantic CSS variables driven by a theme class/data attribute or prefers-color-scheme.

questions.question: Avoid CSS leakage?
questions.answer: Use scoped styles, disciplined naming, CSS Modules or cascade layers and minimize global selectors.

questions.question: Reflow vs repaint?
questions.answer: Reflow/layout recalculates geometry; repaint redraws pixels. Some changes trigger both.

questions.question: Why prefer transform/opacity for many animations?
questions.answer: They can avoid repeated layout calculations and can be handled efficiently by the rendering pipeline; always measure.

questions.question: prefers-reduced-motion?
questions.answer: A media feature allowing users to request reduced animation/motion for accessibility.

questions.question: Design tokens?
questions.answer: Named values for color, spacing, typography, radius and other design decisions that keep a design system consistent.

questions.question: SCSS vs CSS Modules vs component library?
questions.answer: They solve different problems. A component library gives reusable UI behavior; CSS Modules scope styles; SCSS provides preprocessing. A large ERP can combine a design system with scoped component styles.

questions.question: What is a design system?
questions.answer: A coordinated set of design tokens, components, patterns, accessibility rules and documentation.

questions.question: How do you prevent a design system becoming a bottleneck?
questions.answer: Define contribution standards, ownership, versioning and extension points. Keep primitives stable and composable.

questions.question: How do you implement theme switching?
questions.answer: Use semantic tokens and a root theme class/data attribute so components consume variables rather than hard-coded colors.

questions.question: How do you handle responsive ERP layouts?
questions.answer: Use flexible grid/flex layouts, breakpoints and container queries where component-level responsiveness helps.

questions.question: How do you review CSS?
questions.answer: Check semantics, scope, specificity, responsive behavior, accessibility, duplication and whether a value belongs in a shared token/component.

questions.question: What is CSS architecture's biggest goal?
questions.answer: Predictability. A developer should know where a style comes from and how safely it can be changed.
